<samp>RESEARCH COMPENDIUM</samp>

<h1><b><i>Characterizing Core Morphology and Scar Patterning Within a
Unified Spherical Harmonic Framework</i></b></h1>

<hr />

[![Reproducibility
Check](https://github.com/PeiyuanXiao/SPHARM_analysis/actions/workflows/reproducibility.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PeiyuanXiao/SPHARM_analysis/actions/workflows/reproducibility.yml)
[![Project Status: Under
Review](https://www.repostatus.org/badges/latest/active.svg)](https://www.repostatus.org/#active)
[![License:
MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)
[![License: CC BY
4.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License_(text/figures)-CC_BY_4.0-lightgrey.svg)](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

CC0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License_(data)-CC0-green.svg)](http://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)

This repository is the research compendium for the following paper:

> Peiyuan Xiao, Hao Li, Ben Marwick (2026). *Characterizing core
> morphology and scar patterning within a unified spherical harmonic
> framework*. Submitted to *Journal of Archaeological Method and
> Theory*.

The compendium presents a unified spherical harmonic (SPHARM) framework
for jointly characterizing two properties of lithic cores: their
three-dimensional **morphology** (M-SPHARM, derived from surface meshes)
and the spatial structure of their **scar patterning** (SP-SPHARM,
derived from kernel-density estimates of scar orientation vectors on the
sphere). These descriptors are benchmarked against established
scar-pattern metrics (SPI and fabric analysis), tested for rotational
invariance, and applied to both experimental and archaeological core
assemblages.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 📁 Contents

The **analysis** directory contains all materials needed to reproduce
the study:

- [:file_folder: paper](/analysis/paper): Quarto source for the
  manuscript ([`manuscript.qmd`](/analysis/paper/manuscript.qmd)), the
  bibliography (`references.bib`), and the rendered `manuscript.docx`.
  All figures, tables, and in-text statistics are drawn directly from
  the `targets` pipeline via `tar_read()`.

- [:file_folder: data](/analysis/data):

  - `raw_data/` — scar orientation data (`Scar_orientation_data.xlsx`)
    and core metric data (`SDG_core_metric.xlsx`).
  - `3D_models_cores/` — core meshes in `.stl` format (not version
    controlled; see [Data](#data) below).
  - `derived_data/` — intermediate and final output files (power
    spectra, ILR scores, statistical tables); fully regenerated by the
    pipeline.

- [:file_folder: scripts](/analysis/scripts): all analysis code.

  - **SPHARM_main** — pipeline entry points:
    [`SPHARM_main.py`](/analysis/scripts/SPHARM_main/SPHARM_main.py)
    (batch M-SPHARM of core meshes) and
    [`kde_to_spharm_main.py`](/analysis/scripts/SPHARM_main/kde_to_spharm_main.py)
    (scar vectors → von Mises-Fisher KDE → SP-SPHARM).
  - **SPHARM_modules** — supporting Python modules for mesh
    preprocessing, PCA alignment, SPHARM computation and power spectra,
    von Mises-Fisher KDE, and shape reconstruction.
  - **r_alignment / r_spharm / r_statistics / r_validation / r_utils** —
    R scripts for scar vector alignment, power degree selection,
    statistical analysis, method and rotation validation, and shared
    utilities.
  - `environment.yml` — the conda environment (`spharm`) for all Python
    steps.

- [:file_folder: output](/analysis/output): figures and other
  illustrations generated by the pipeline (not version controlled).

- [:file_folder: figures](/analysis/figures): PNG copies of every figure
  in the manuscript and supplementary materials.

- [:file_folder: templates](/analysis/templates): Quarto/Pandoc
  templates, the Word reference document, and the citation style (CSL).

The pipeline is defined in [`_targets.R`](/_targets.R) at the project
root. It orchestrates three stages, **R preprocessing → Python SPHARM →
R statistics**, as a single reproducible
[`targets`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) workflow.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 🗄️ Data {#data}

The complete research compendium, including all code and data required
to reproduce the study, is archived in the project's public OSF
repository (<https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/d82c5>), which provides a
citable, versioned snapshot; this GitHub repository is the live
development version. The scar orientation and core metric data are
version-controlled here under `analysis/data/raw_data/`.

The 3D core meshes (`.stl` files) are too large for version control and
are distributed through OSF as `3D_models_cores.zip`. Download it from
the OSF archive and unzip it into `analysis/data/` — the archive
contains a `3D_models_cores/` folder, so the meshes land at:

```         
analysis/data/3D_models_cores/
```

so that each core mesh (e.g. `EXP01_Levallois preferential.stl`) sits
directly in that folder.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 🚀 How to Reproduce the Analysis in a Docker Container

This compendium ships a [Dockerfile](Dockerfile) that builds the
complete computational environment: R 4.4.2 with RStudio and all
required R packages (restored from `renv.lock`), plus the conda `spharm`
environment for the Python SPHARM steps. Because both stacks are bundled
in a single image, the entire workflow can be reproduced with a single
`targets::tar_make()` call; the Python scripts do not need to be run
manually.

**Step 1: Install [Docker](https://www.docker.com/get-started/)** on
your computer.

**Step 2: Get the compendium.** Clone the repository:

```         
git clone https://github.com/PeiyuanXiao/SPHARM_analysis.git
```

or download the ZIP from GitHub (green `< > Code` button →
`Download ZIP`) and unzip it.

**Step 3: Add the 3D models.** Download `3D_models_cores` from the [data
archive](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/d82c5) (see [Data](#data)) and
place the `.stl` files in `analysis/data/3D_models_cores/`.

**Step 4: Build the Docker image.** Run the following from the project
root (note the trailing `.`). This step may take some time, as it
restores all R packages and resolves the conda environment:

```         
docker build --platform=linux/amd64 -t spharm_analysis .
```

> **Note (Apple Silicon Macs):** The Dockerfile pins the base image to
> `linux/amd64`, the reference platform used for validation. On Apple
> Silicon Macs, Docker will run the image under emulation, which is
> slower but keeps the computational platform consistent. Native arm64
> builds are not the documented reproduction path for this compendium.

On OSX you may need to run:

```         
docker build --platform=linux/amd64 -t spharm_analysis .
```

**Step 5: Start the container.** The simplest approach is via Docker
Compose, which maps port 8787 and mounts the project at `/project`:

```         
docker compose up -d
```

Alternatively, with plain Docker:

*Linux/macOS:*

```         
docker run -d -p 8787:8787 -v $(pwd):/project -w /project -e PASSWORD=rstudio spharm_analysis
```

*Windows (Git Bash):*

```         
MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 docker run -d -p 8787:8787 -v $(pwd):/project -w /project -e PASSWORD=rstudio spharm_analysis
```

**Step 6: Open RStudio.** Navigate to <http://localhost:8787/> in your
browser and log in with username `rstudio` and password `rstudio`. The
project opens automatically at `/project`.

**Step 7: Run the pipeline and reproduction report.** You can do this in
one command, or interactively step by step.

*Option A: one command (recommended).* From `/project` inside the
container, `make.R` runs the full pipeline and then renders the
reproduction report in sequence:

```         
Rscript make.R
```

*Option B: step by step, in the R console.* First run the pipeline:

``` r
targets::tar_make()
```

then render the reproduction report yourself:

```         
quarto render analysis/paper/reproduction_report.qmd
```

Either way, `tar_make()` executes every stage in dependency order and
only recomputes out-of-date targets:

- **Stage 1 (in R):** align scar direction vectors.
- **Stage 2 (in Python):** batch M-SPHARM of core meshes, and spherical
  KDE → SP-SPHARM of scar vectors. Python targets run as separate
  processes against the conda `spharm` environment.
- **Stage 3 (in R):** power degree selection, method comparison (SPI /
  fabric / SP-SPHARM), rotational-invariance validation, and statistical
  analyses of the experimental and SDG core assemblages.

The **reproduction report** is a single self-contained HTML capturing
the *complete statistical output* `tar_make()` prints (organised by
module) alongside the pipeline graph; the manuscript reports only a
subset of these results for space, so this is the full record for
reviewers.

To build a single target and its dependencies, use e.g.
`targets::tar_make(spharm_analysis)`. To see the whole pipeline as a
labelled flow chart — each step annotated with the analysis it performs
— run `targets::tar_visnetwork()`.

**Step 8: Render the manuscript.** The paper is a Quarto document whose
prose is interwoven with code that reads results directly from the
pipeline. After the pipeline completes, render it to a Word document:

```         
quarto render analysis/paper/manuscript.qmd --to docx
```

**Step 9: View the output:**

``` r
browseURL("analysis/paper/manuscript.docx")
```

**Step 10: Clean up.** When finished, stop and remove the container:

```         
docker compose down
```

Or, if you started it with `docker run`:

```         
docker ps -aq | xargs docker stop | xargs docker rm
```
